v.why: At tiny learning rates the net is already undertrained in 243 epochs, so extra shrinkage competes with fitting.
Very wide nets have excess capacity to overfit, so stronger L2 acts as useful capacity control.
The L2 term is divided by batch size in sklearn-style MLPs, so small batches feel alpha far more strongly and underfit sooner, on top of already having noise regularization.
The stable learning-rate window shrinks with width, so wider nets diverge sooner at large step sizes.
A single hidden layer is a width bottleneck, so more units substitute for missing depth.
Narrow nets lack capacity that extra layers supply by substitution.
Large batches give few updates under a fixed epoch budget, and deeper nets need more updates to optimize.
Since the L2 term is divided by batch size, larger batches weaken the effective penalty and relieve underfitting from strong alpha.
Shallow nets have a wide stable learning-rate window and gain from faster progress.
Large batches take few steps under a fixed epoch budget, so a larger step size compensates.
